title: Evidence-Based Reasoning
author: Chrys Dougherty
summary: Chrys Dougherty, in the third post of a series on educating informed citizens for a liberal democracy, argues that critical thinking is really evidence-based reasoning and that it cannot be separated from knowledge of the subject. He holds that reasoning skills do not transfer automatically across domains, so students need deep subject knowledge to spot implausible claims, ask good questions and understand what counts as evidence in history versus physics. He then lists six kinds of general knowledge that help: ground rules for testing claims, checking sources, statistical reasoning, cognitive biases, specious arguments and propaganda, and the value of differing opinions. He stresses that even knowledgeable people often choose not to follow the evidence, so willingness, epistemic humility and curiosity are habits that must be cultivated. For schools, he recommends a knowledge-rich, question-asking curriculum with balanced discussion of controversial topics, plus efforts to help parents see how reasoning expectations show up in assignments. He closes with books by Rauch, Stanovich, and Caulfield and Wineburg as further reading.
points: Critical thinking is not a portable skill set: the author argues that thinking well about a subject requires knowing it, so a knowledge-rich curriculum is the precondition for teaching reasoning.
Knowing a subject lets students judge what experts mean, flag unlikely statements, generate questions and understand the type of evidence each discipline accepts.
Cognitive biases such as myside bias, motivated reasoning and aversion to complexity mean that having the knowledge is not enough, and following the evidence is a habit of will to be cultivated.
The 'free inquiry with competitive testing of ideas' model, requiring falsifiable claims and repeatable tests, explains why diversity of opinion makes knowledge more reliable.
Schools can signal success by whether students and adults avoid invalid arguments, respect differing views, and seek the knowledge needed for evidence-informed opinions.
quotes: What is involved in helping current and future citizens become good critical thinkers? What’s important is that they can think critically with evidence. Thinking without evidence is often not helpful.
Evidence-based reasoning is not a set of skills that can be learned once with the confidence that they can be applied in any subject. To think well about a subject you have to know about it!
Even when people know enough about a subject to use evidence well, they often choose not to. Humans are prone to cognitive biases, predictable errors that occur because it is convenient to make them.

To be testable, claims must be clearly defined and must be falsifiable—it must be clear what kinds of evidence would show that the claim is wrong. Testing includes looking for contradictory as well as supporting evidence.
Individuals and institutions are likely to be more reliable sources of information when their reputations depend on their accuracy and their willingness to correct mistakes when they are wrong.
People often engage in wishful thinking—they decide emotionally what they want to believe and then look for evidence that supports those beliefs while downplaying contradictory evidence.
All humans have cognitive biases, but those with different biases are more likely to check each other. To paraphrase James Madison, “Bias must be made to counteract bias.

The first requirement for teaching evidence-based reasoning is a knowledge-rich curriculum to give students information from which to draw evidence and to teach them how evidence is gathered and used in different subjects.
